title: The Intuitive Dog and Its Rational Tail
coreMove: Treat a moral reason as an advocate's brief until you know which intuition hired it.
sourcePressure: The chapter makes the intuition-first claim directly: moral reasoning often justifies and persuades after intuition has already moved.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer makes reason useless instead of showing reason as socially powerful but often post-hoc.

sourceAnchors.name: David Hume
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar makes Hume central because he treats reason as serving the passions, with Haidt preferring servant language.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Hume belongs in the room whenever a tidy reason arrives after the emotional verdict has already taken its seat.

sourceAnchors.name: Antonio Damasio
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar lists Damasio among the support surface for returning morality toward emotion and intuition.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Damasio's work gives the chapter permission to treat feeling as part of judgment, not as noise outside it.

sourceAnchors.name: Frans de Waal
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar names de Waal in the support surface for emotion, automaticity, and social moral life.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: De Waal keeps morality from looking like a late classroom invention; social feeling has older roots.

hook: Do not open ch02 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital morbidity review after a risky but successful shortcut
exampleSpecs.audience: clinicians defending their judgments under scrutiny
exampleSpecs.stakes: Emily hears polished reasons arrive after a gut-level loyalty response.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Emily writes the first emotional verdict on the board before allowing anyone to list clinical reasons.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "We would do it again," the surgeon says before anyone opens the case file.

exampleSpecs.domain: product team deciding whether a disliked feature is unethical or merely ugly
exampleSpecs.audience: design leads with strong taste reactions
exampleSpecs.stakes: Chris must find the intuition underneath his principled language.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Chris deletes three noble-sounding objections and names the embarrassment he felt when users mocked the prototype.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The prototype loops silently on a wall monitor while nobody sits in the front row.

exampleSpecs.domain: parent-teacher conference after a playground exclusion
exampleSpecs.audience: teachers mediating parents who each feel morally certain
exampleSpecs.stakes: Manon catches both parents using fairness language to defend their own child first.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Manon asks each parent to state the other child's strongest reason before giving another defense.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Wet mittens drip under the conference table as two parents speak over each other.

exampleSpecs.domain: investment committee rejecting a proposal from a rival office
exampleSpecs.audience: finance partners protecting reputation through analysis
exampleSpecs.stakes: Yusuf spots the memo becoming an advocate for office pride.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Yusuf compares the rejection memo with last year's identical risk that the committee accepted from its own team.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Yusuf one archived memo to see that the spreadsheet had learned office politics.

exampleSpecs.domain: climate nonprofit choosing campaign language after donor backlash
exampleSpecs.audience: campaign strategists who believe they are just following evidence
exampleSpecs.stakes: Pavel notices that donor identity selected the evidence the team called decisive.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 10:12, Pavel asks the team to predict which fact each donor group will call most rational before showing the split.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 10:12, Pavel dims the screen and leaves only the donor segments visible.

exampleSpecs.domain: couple deciding whether a holiday visit is fair
exampleSpecs.audience: readers in intimate arguments where reasons arrive fast
exampleSpecs.stakes: Grace identifies the feeling of being taken for granted before continuing the fairness debate.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You pause with the calendar open and say the feeling first, then ask whether the fairness reason still fits.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You have the shared calendar open and your thumb over the send button.

skillTargets: identify post-hoc reasoning after an intuitive verdict
separate persuasion and justification from neutral truth seeking
recognize when emotion is part of judgment rather than a contaminant

tryThisNowSpec: In your next disagreement, pause after your first reason and ask, 'What feeling is this reason protecting?'
